prompt: You set a maximum of 50 output tokens. What does the model do differently?
hint: Does the model know the limit exists?

choices.text: Nothing; the loop is stopped at 50
choices.why: Right. The model writes as it would have, and generation is cut when the count is reached.

choices.text: It plans an answer that fits in 50 tokens
choices.why: The model never sees the limit, so it cannot plan around it.

choices.text: It writes faster, so that it finishes in time
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it. The limit is a count, not a clock.

choices.text: It summarises its answer to fit
choices.why: Summarising would need the model to know the limit. Ask for brevity in the prompt instead.

hint: There are two reasons generation stops.

choices.text: The model chose to end the text
choices.why: That is printed as `end`.

choices.text: The output was as long as the prompt
choices.why: The prompt's length does not decide when output stops.

choices.text: The answer was complete and the right length
choices.why: `length` says nothing about completeness. Often the answer was cut.

choices.text: The loop hit the token limit
choices.why: Right. The model did not choose to stop; the count reached `--max-tokens`.

prompt: `toylm generate "the menu has" --temperature 0 --max-tokens 3` printed `soup, bread`. How many tokens did the uncut answer have?
hint: Read the run without a tight limit.

prompt: Why is `the menu has soup, bread` a dangerous output?
hint: Compare it with the uncut answer.

choices.text: It is ungrammatical, so a reader will be confused by it
choices.why: It is grammatical, which is exactly the problem.

choices.text: It reads as complete and is false
choices.why: Right. The menu also has cake, and a cut list rarely looks cut. Only the finish reason says so.

choices.text: It came from a temperature above 0
choices.why: It was written at temperature 0. The limit cut it.

choices.text: Bread is not on the menu
choices.why: Bread is on the menu. Cake is the item that was cut off.

prompt: At temperature 0, `toylm` writes `sleeps and the cat sleeps and the cat...` after `the cat` until the limit. Why does it never stop on its own?
hint: Follow the top word in each pair.

choices.text: The corpus has no full stop after `sleeps`
choices.why: It does: `the cat sleeps on the chair by the window .` The full stop is just never the top choice on this path.

choices.text: The likeliest words form a circle that never reaches the end
choices.why: Right: `sleeps` → `and` → `the` → `cat` → `sleeps`. Greedy decoding takes the same turn every time.

choices.text: Temperature 0 disables the end token
choices.why: The end token can win at temperature 0; `the café opens at` ends after `seven.`

choices.text: The default limit is too high
choices.why: The limit is what stops it. Without the circle, it would end well before.

prompt: Your program asks for a JSON object and parses the reply. Sometimes parsing fails with an unterminated string. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

choices.text: The limit cut the object; raise it and check the finish reason
choices.why: Right. A cut object is not JSON. Leave room above the largest reply, and treat `length` as a failure to handle.

choices.text: The model does not know JSON; switch to plain text and parse it yourself
choices.why: The complete reply was valid. The failure came from where the loop was stopped.

choices.text: The schema is wrong; loosen it so that more replies pass
choices.why: `validate` refused it before reaching the schema: it was not JSON at all.

choices.text: The temperature is too high, so it writes broken syntax
choices.why: A cut at the limit happens at any temperature, including 0.

prompt: `tok count reply.json` reported how many tokens for the complete JSON reply?
Which of these should code that calls a model do with a finish reason of `length`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Treat the reply as possibly incomplete
choices.why: Yes. That is what the value says.

choices.text: Retry with a higher limit, or report an error
choices.why: Yes. Both handle the cut instead of passing it on.

choices.text: Parse the reply as if it were complete
choices.why: That is how a cut list becomes a false fact downstream.

choices.text: Ignore it when the text looks finished
choices.why: A cut answer rarely looks cut, so how it looks is no evidence.

prompt: Why does an output limit bound the cost of a request?
hint: What happens when the count reaches the limit?

choices.text: The provider refunds any tokens written past the limit
choices.why: No tokens are written past it. Generation stops.

choices.text: The model writes cheaper tokens near the limit
choices.why: Every output token has the same price.

choices.text: Generation stops there, so output never runs past it
choices.why: Right. Limit times the output price is the ceiling on what one request's output costs.

choices.text: It lowers the price of every input token in the request
choices.why: Input is priced separately and does not change.

prompt: In `tok cost`, 79 input tokens at 2 per million and 40 output tokens at 8 per million. Which part costs more?

choices.text: The input, since there are almost twice as many input tokens
choices.why: Count is only half of it; the price per token is four times higher for output.

choices.text: The output, at about twice the input
choices.why: Right: 0.000320 against 0.000158. Fewer tokens, and still the bigger share, because each costs four times as much.

choices.text: They cost the same
choices.why: They do not: the two lines differ by a factor of two.

choices.text: It depends on the temperature
choices.why: Temperature does not appear in the price.

prompt: With the illustrative prices and 400 output tokens, `tok cost` gave what total for 10,000 requests?
hint: The last line of the second run.

prompt: A request has a limit of 400 output tokens, at an illustrative 8 per million. What is the most its output can cost?

choices.why: That is the input of the example request, not the output bound.

choices.text: Nothing can be said until the reply arrives
choices.why: The limit sets a ceiling in advance. That is what makes it a budget.
That is ten thousand requests, input included.
Right: 400 × 8 / 1,000,000. Whatever the model does, it cannot write more than 400 tokens.

prompt: What does asking for "one sentence" in the prompt do that the limit cannot?
hint: One changes what is written, the other where it is cut.

choices.text: It guarantees the reply stays under the limit
choices.why: An instruction is followed often and not always. The limit is the guarantee.

choices.text: It makes the request cheaper per token
choices.why: The price per token is fixed by the provider.

choices.text: Nothing; both do the same job
choices.why: They do different jobs, which is why the section says to use both.

choices.text: It moves the model towards a short, complete answer
choices.why: Right. The limit only stops a long answer part-way through.

prompt: A team sets a tight limit and removes "reply briefly" from the prompt to save input tokens. What should they expect?
hint: What does a limit without an instruction produce?

choices.text: Shorter, complete replies, because the model sees the limit
choices.why: The model never sees the limit.

choices.text: A higher bill per request
choices.why: The limit still caps output. What they lose is completeness, not money.

choices.text: More replies cut part-way, ending in `length`
choices.why: Right. The model writes at its usual length and the limit chops it; the saving on input buys broken output.

choices.text: No change, since instructions are ignored
choices.why: Instructions change what is likely. Removing one changes the replies.

prompt: Order these steps for setting the output limit of a classification request that replies in JSON.
hint: Measure first, then decide, then check.
items: Write the instruction asking for the object and nothing else
Measure the largest valid reply with a tokenizer
Set the limit a little above that size
Check the finish reason of every reply before parsing

prompt: When a reply stops because the limit was reached, `toylm` prints `finish: ___`.
hint: One word; the other value is `end`.

prompt: Match each observation to what it tells you.

pairs.right: the loop was cut at the limit
an object was cut before it closed
what an unbounded reply costs at scale

right_distractors: the model was told about the limit
